title: Eight Central Banks Holding a Price: a Cumulative Deficit of 3,692 Million, and the Pool Disbanded on 15 March 1968

extractionLoop.stage1_upfrontSkim: What was spent was reserves, to hold a number. After a run sent the London price to $40 an ounce on 20 October 1960, the Pool was formed on 1 November 1961 by eight central banks, which "agreed to pool gold reserves to intervene in the London gold market in order to maintain the Bretton Woods system" and keep the price at $35. In the NBER paper's words, verified on a parallel branch, "Major central banks pooled interventions – sharing profits and losses – to stabilize the dollar price of gold", and "The Bank of England started operations for the gold consortium on November 6, 1961."
extractionLoop.stage2_structuralCompromise: The compromise was the promise itself: since 1958 "countries settled their international balances in dollars, and U.S. dollars were convertible to gold at a fixed exchange rate of $35 an ounce", with the United States responsible for keeping that price fixed. A convertibility pledge is only as good as the metal behind it — and the Pool defended the price by selling the members' own metal into the market whenever it rose, which gave the defence a quantity limit nobody had agreed in advance.
extractionLoop.stage3_informationFog: The intervention was the fog: a price maintained by coordinated central bank selling looks, to anyone reading the quote, like a market price. What the quote did not show is in the NBER paper: "From the end of 1965 to March 1968, the cumulative deficit was 3692 million." The Federal Reserve essay records the parallel machinery of swap lines with nine central banks providing "up to $900 million equivalent in foreign exchange", and notes that "What started as a small, short-term credit facility grew to be a large, intermediate-term facility" — a temporary fix that was "a sign of a fundamental problem in the monetary system".
extractionLoop.stage4_monopolyWindfall: The arrangement bought seven years. "The pool was successful for six years until another gold crisis ensued", and in that time the dollar's convertibility was treated as sound because its price did not move.
extractionLoop.stage5_merseyWhitewash: The ending was a two-tier price rather than an admission. Sterling devalued, a run on gold followed, France withdrew, and — in the NBER paper's dating — "On March 15, 1968, the Gold Pool was disbanded and a two-tier arrangement put in its place." The seven remaining members "agreed to formulate a two-tiered system", with central banks using gold only to settle international debts — one price for governments and another for everyone else. The gold window closed entirely in August 1971.

closedLoopRatchet.inheritedFramework: Bretton Woods: fixed currencies against the dollar and the dollar fixed to gold at $35, with the United States carrying the convertibility obligation for the system, defended in London by a consortium of the countries that held the gold.
closedLoopRatchet.newFrameworkCreated: The two-tier gold market of March 1968 — an official price preserved among monetary authorities and a private price left to supply and demand — and then the closing of the gold window in August 1971, the end of the convertibility the Pool had been built to defend.
closedLoopRatchet.closedLoopRecirculation: Defending the price required selling reserves; selling reserves reduced the backing that made the price credible; the weaker the backing, the more the price had to be defended, until a cumulative deficit of 3,692 million ended it. A price guaranteed with the members' own reserves was abandoned to the market at the point the reserves ran short, and retained for the members themselves. The swap lines meant to bridge the gap grew into a standing facility, which the Federal Reserve's own essay reads as the symptom rather than the cure.

decoyVsLedger.viralDecoy: That the gold price was secretly rigged by a cartel of central banks and the public was never told; or, from the other direction, that the Pool was simply overwhelmed by speculators who broke the central banks.
decoyVsLedger.whyDecoyFails: The price was indeed held by coordinated central bank intervention — but not secretly, and the source for that is a Federal Reserve publication stating it plainly: the London Gold Pool "was formed on November 1, 1961", consisted of eight named central banks, and "agreed to pool gold reserves to intervene in the London gold market in order to maintain the Bretton Woods system" and keep gold at $35 an ounce. An arrangement whose membership, date, mechanism and purpose are published by one of its members is a policy, not a conspiracy. The "overwhelmed by speculators" version fails on the arithmetic the NBER paper supplies: a cumulative deficit of 3,692 million between the end of 1965 and March 1968 is the members' own metal going out the door, and the Pool was "disbanded" on 15 March 1968 — a decision, with a two-tier arrangement "put in its place" — rather than defeated in the market. What the record supports is the thing both decoys gesture at without naming: the price people could observe was an administered price, it was administered until it could not be, and when it failed the response kept one price for central banks and let the other float. A LIMIT STATED PLAINLY: the parallel session's version of this node rested its sharpest claim — the G10 governors' own words at the Washington meeting of 16 March 1968, that "henceforth officially held gold should be used only to effect transfers among monetary authorities" — on the BIS 38th Annual Report of 1968. On 18 October 2026 that URL and every alternative path tried on bis.org returned 404, so the citation could not be re-verified and is not carried, and those words are not in this dossier. The two-tier fact rests here on the Federal Reserve essay and the NBER paper. ON SOURCING: the Federal Reserve History essay was read here; the NBER paper was fetched and verified through glm-recheck --strict-sources on a parallel branch and is carried with that stated in its citation. Both are secondary, and the dossier is tiered accordingly.
decoyVsLedger.documentedLedger: A run that sent the London gold price to $40 an ounce on 20 October 1960. The London Gold Pool formed on 1 November 1961 by eight central banks — Great Britain, West Germany, Switzerland, the Netherlands, Belgium, Italy, France and the United States — pooling reserves, "sharing profits and losses", to hold the price at $35, with the Bank of England starting operations for the consortium on 6 November 1961. Parallel swap lines with nine central banks providing up to $900 million equivalent, which grew from a short-term facility into an intermediate-term one. Success for six years. A cumulative deficit of 3,692 million from the end of 1965 to March 1968. Then sterling's devaluation, another run on gold, France's withdrawal, the Pool disbanded on 15 March 1968 and a two-tier arrangement put in its place, in which the seven remaining members used gold only to settle international debts. Convertibility ended altogether in August 1971. The 1 November 1961 formation date is the Federal Reserve essay's; the 6 November 1961 start of operations is the NBER paper's; they are not in conflict.

citations.title: Federal Reserve History, "Nixon Ends Convertibility of U.S. Dollars to Gold and Announces Wage/Price Controls, August 1971", by Sandra Kollen Ghizoni
citations.quoteOrFact: Read from federalreservehistory.org. NOTE ON FIT: the essay's subject is August 1971, not March 1968. It is cited here because it contains the passage on the London Gold Pool, which is this node's subject, and nothing in this dossier is drawn from the essay beyond what it says about the Pool and the system around it. On the system: under Bretton Woods "countries agreed to keep their currencies fixed (but adjustable in exceptional situations) to the dollar, and the dollar was fixed to gold. Since 1958 ... countries settled their international balances in dollars, and U.S. dollars were convertible to gold at a fixed exchange rate of $35 an ounce." ON THE POOL ITSELF: "A run in the London gold market sent the price to $40 an ounce on October 20, 1960, exacerbating the threat to the system. In response, the London Gold Pool was formed on November 1, 1961. The pool consisted of a group of eight central banks (Great Britain, West Germany, Switzerland, the Netherlands, Belgium, Italy, France, and the United States). In order to keep the price of gold at $35 an ounce, the group agreed to pool gold reserves to intervene in the London gold market in order to maintain the Bretton Woods system. The pool was successful for six years until another gold crisis ensued. The British pound sterling devalued and another run on gold occurred, and France withdrew from the pool. The pool collapsed in March 1968. At that time the seven remaining members of the London Gold Pool ... agreed to formulate a two-tiered system." On the swap lines that ran alongside it: credit lines with nine central banks "provided up to $900 million equivalent in foreign exchange", and "What started as a small, short-term credit facility grew to be a large, intermediate-term facility until the U.S. gold window closed in August 1971. The growth and need for the swap lines signaled that they were not just a temporary fix, but a sign of a fundamental problem in the monetary system." SOURCE CHARACTER: Federal Reserve History is an educational project of the Federal Reserve System. This is a signed secondary essay with its own bibliography, not a primary record, and it is tiered and attributed accordingly: the dossier says what the essay states, not what a contemporaneous document shows.
